_about: The peace hub (plan 7.6f), built to the level of love and righteousness. Peace is one Hebrew word, שָׁלוֹם, that the Berean renders 'peace' 149 times and otherwise 'welfare', 'well', 'all right', 'safe', 'safely', 'prosperity', 'greet' and more: it is also the greeting, the question 'Is it well?', and a man's well-being. The Greek εἰρήνη renders it in the Greek Old Testament and carries the greeting into the letters. The sense rule therefore keeps every sense of these words, and the rows show the senses apart (greeting and welfare, safety, peace between parties, peace as the LORD's gift, what peace stands beside) instead of folding them into the one English word. Rows as in love.json and righteousness.json; match 'all' (a verse sits in every row it fits); 'pick' where the idiom is a whole phrase (the Hebrew 'Go in peace', 'Do you come in peace?', 'Is it well?') and no companion word marks it. Built by tools/concepts/hub_build.py. REGROUPED (coordinator's rule 8, 15-25 rows): a first build had 53 rows; rows that say one kind of thing were merged, every contested row and its note kept, every divine-person row kept by pick, and no verse left the hub (a verse leaving a row stands in a broader row or in 'Peace in other uses'). Where merged rows had different rules (a row's conditions are ANDed, so two rules cannot share a row), the merged row is a pick list taken from the rule build of 2026-10-10, each verse still one the rule had found.
_words_why: שָׁלוֹם and εἰρήνη are the one word across the testaments (the Greek Old Testament renders the one by the other), with the Aramaic שְׁלָם (Ezra 5:7 'All peace'; Dan 4:1) and the Greek family (εἰρηνεύω live at peace, εἰρηνικός peaceable, εἰρηνοποιέω make peace, εἰρηνοποιός peacemaker). The verb שָׁלַם is 'repay, pay, restore, finish' in all but a dozen verses ('made peace with', 'at peace with'); the sense rule keeps only those. שַׁלְוָה (the card's third word) is a different root (שׁלה, ease, quiet, complacency) and goes with the other words the English renders 'peace', not with the rows; שֶׁלֶם 'peace offering' likewise. The builder files שָׁלַם as a noun, so its verses stand in noun rows, by hand.
_sense_why: Not 'peace' alone: that would hide the greeting and the welfare of שָׁלוֹם (the verses MACULA glosses 'welfare', 'well', 'all right', 'safe', 'prosperity', 'greet'...) and show the reader that the word is only the opposite of war. The alternatives the regex admits are the glosses actually given to these words; it also admits the dozen verses of שָׁלַם that mean 'made peace' and nothing of its 'repay' (no such gloss matches).

others._why: Words the English renders 'peace' that are not שָׁלוֹם and εἰρήνη: שֶׁלֶם 'peace offering' (the Berean mostly says 'fellowship offering'), שַׁלְוָה 'ease', ἄμαχος 'peaceable'. Named apart with their verses; the reader is never handed one as the other. h4993 is a gloss stray; h7951 (Job 12:6, 'safe') is one verse the Berean does not render 'peace'; h1585 גְּמַר (Ezra 7:12) is MACULA's gloss 'peace' where the Berean prints 'Greetings' (panel fix: the title says 'translated peace'; the verse stands in the wish row's company, not here).
others.title: Other words translated “peace”

3John.1.15.why: the Greek's 3 John 1:15 ('Peace to you') is printed in the Berean's 1:14, whose 1:15 is empty

rows.label: The wish of peace: “Peace to you”, “All peace”, “Grace and peace to you”

not_verses.Rom.16.20: 'the God of peace will soon crush Satan' and 'the grace of our Lord' are two separate closing wishes; peace and grace are not wished together

rows.note: The opening wish of the letters, kept as written, with the same wish spoken in Hebrew and Aramaic: 'Peace to you', 'Peace be with you', a king's letter ('All peace', 'May your prosperity be multiplied'), and the disciples' 'Peace to this house'. It is listed apart from the rows that say what grace or mercy does.
rows._why: merged from five rows: the letters' wish (rule: χάρις or ἔλεος in the verse) and, by add, the 'Peace to you' verses (by hand: someone says or is told to say peace to another), 'let your peace rest on the house', and the Aramaic שְׁלָם letters

rows.label: “Peace be with you”, “Peace I leave with you”, said by Jesus
rows.note: The first four name Jesus as the speaker. John 14:27 and 16:33 are in His farewell speech to the disciples (John 13-17).
rows._why: by hand, as the divine persons are; merged from two rows

rows.label: “In peace”: go, be sent, come, die
rows.note: The Hebrew בְּשָׁלוֹם and Greek εἰς εἰρήνην, 'in peace', after a verb of going, sending, returning, coming or dying: 'Go in peace', 'Do you come in peace?' and its answer, 'gathered to your fathers in peace'. Jas 2:16 is the text's own example of saying it and doing nothing.
rows._why: by hand; merged from three rows (go, come, die); Luke 2:29 'dismiss Your servant in peace' stands here because the verse does not say death

rows.label: Asked after, greeted: “Is it well?”, “All is well”
rows.note: The same Hebrew word, שָׁלוֹם: the Berean gives it as 'well', 'all right', 'welfare', 'how they were doing' or 'greet'. It is the greeting and the question after someone's health as well as the opposite of war.
rows._why: by hand, from the glosses MACULA gives the word in these verses ('welfare', 'well', 'all right', 'fare', 'greet', 'health') and the Berean's text; Gen 43:23 'It is fine' is the steward's answer to their fear

rows.label: Safe, secure; welfare, well-being, prosperity
rows.note: Deut 23:6 and Ezra 9:12 are commands not to seek the peace or prosperity of Ammon, Moab and the peoples of the land.
rows._why: by hand: the verses where the Berean renders the word 'safe', 'safely', 'safety', 'secure', 'unscathed', or 'welfare', 'well-being', 'prosperity', 'soundness'; merged from two rows (Judg 8:9 and 11:31 'in triumph' are the same Hebrew and stay in 'Peace in other uses', where the Berean's word differs)

rows.label: The heart and the mind; lie down, dwell in a peaceful place
rows._why: merged from two rows: peace beside heart and mind (rule on καρδία, νοῦς, νόημα, φρόνημα, with Isa 26:3 by hand; 2 Tim 2:22 'a pure heart' was taken out as not where peace is) and the picture of lying down and dwelling

rows.label: Peace and war, the sword, enemies; a time of peace

not_verses.2Sam.11.7: שָׁלוֹם here is 'how Joab was doing' (welfare); the war is only what David asks about
not_verses.1Chr.18.10: 'greet' David; the war is the one just fought
not_verses.2Sam.8.10: 'greet' David; the war is the one just fought
not_verses.1Sam.17.22: he asked how they were doing; the battle line is where he ran
not_verses.Jer.38.4: 'the warriors who remain' are those being discouraged; peace here is the people's well-being
not_verses.1Chr.12.18: the Hebrew word counted ('adversaries') belongs to the neighbouring verse in the original's numbering; the Berean's verse has none

rows._why: merged from two rows: war, sword and enemies in the verse (rule) and 'a time of peace' (by hand: peace as the condition of a land or reign, 'peacetime', 'peace on all sides', 'peace and security in my lifetime')

rows.label: Peace made between: an offer of peace, a covenant of peace, make peace with, at peace with
rows.note: Also the Hebrew idiom 'men of your peace', which the Berean gives as 'allies', 'close friend', 'trusted friends', or (Ps 37:37, Luke 10:6) 'a man of peace'. Job 5:23 and 22:21 are Eliphaz speaking to Job.
rows._why: merged from five rows: an offer of peace and peace between (by hand); a covenant of peace (rule: בְּרִית beside the word); the verb שָׁלַם 'make peace' and 'be at peace' (the builder files it with the nouns); the friends and allies. Job 22:21 is also in 'Peace with God'

rows.label: Peace on the earth, peace in heaven
rows.note: Luke 2:14 and Matt 10:34 are set side by side, as the text has them; the page takes no side on how they fit.
rows._why: the Greek γῆ 'earth' only: Luke 2:14, 12:51, Matt 10:34, Rev 6:4, with Luke 19:38 'peace in heaven' by hand. The Hebrew אֶרֶץ 'land' is not used as a rule here because it is also the land of Egypt, of Judah, in verses about welfare

rows.label: “There is no peace”; “Peace, peace,” when there is none
rows.note: Peace missing, taken away, hoped for and not come; and peace announced where it is not. Jer 28:9 is the test the text gives for the second.
rows._why: by hand; merged from two rows

rows.label: Speak, proclaim, preach peace; the gospel of peace; good news
rows._why: merged from two rows: speaking peace (by hand) and good news and salvation (rule: εὐαγγέλιον, εὐαγγελίζω, בָּשַׂר, יְשׁוּעָה...), whose five verses were all already here

rows.label: From the LORD, from God: the God of peace, the peace of God, “The LORD Is Peace”
rows.note: Given, blessed, established, spoken, taken away: what the verses say the LORD does with peace; and the text's own phrases, kept as written ('the God of peace', 'the peace of God', 'the Lord of peace', the altar named 'The LORD Is Peace'). The page does not say more than the verses do about whose peace this is. Isa 45:7 sets it beside calamity: 'I bring prosperity and create calamity'. Ps 147:14, 'He makes peace at your borders', follows 'Exalt the LORD, O Jerusalem' (147:12). Job 25:2 is Bildad speaking.
rows._why: by hand, as the divine persons are: only verses where the text itself names the LORD or God (Ps 147:14 joined from the 'He' row by the panel's fix: 147:12 names the LORD); merged from three rows, one of which had been a rule (with @divine, adjacent) and is now the same verses by pick

rows.label: The ruler from Bethlehem, the king who comes to Zion, the servant: “He will be our peace”, “He will proclaim peace”
rows.note: The text says “He”. In Micah he is the ruler from Bethlehem (5:2) who shepherds in the strength of the LORD (5:4); in Zechariah, the king who comes to Zion (9:9); in Isaiah 53:5, “the punishment that brought us peace was upon Him”, the servant. Christian readers take these of Christ; Jewish readers read them of a king of David's line, of the Messiah, or (Isaiah 53) of Israel. The page does not choose.
rows._why: panel fix: the old 'He' row filed these Hebrew verses under a note that closed on Christ and a door to Jesus. Each passage has its own antecedent in its context, so the label uses the passage's own terms and the only door is Messiah

rows.label: In Christ, through Jesus Christ: “He Himself is our peace”
rows.note: Ephesians 2:13 names Christ Jesus; the verses speak of Him making the two one. Ephesians 2:15 says “abolishing in His flesh the law of commandments and decrees”; readers part on what is abolished, and the page takes no side.
rows._why: by hand: verses that name Christ or Jesus beside peace ('through Jesus Christ', 'in Christ', 'the peace of Christ'), with Eph 2:14-15 (Christ named at 2:13) moved here from the 'He' row and from the law row by the panel's fixes

rows.label: “Peace with God”
rows.note: Rom 5:1 says “we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ”, after “justified through faith”; Isa 27:5 “make peace with Me”; Job 22:21 “be at peace with Him”. In Romans 5:1 the Greek reads “let us have peace” (ἔχωμεν) and the Berean prints “we have peace”. Job 22:21 is Eliphaz speaking to Job. Where readers part on what this peace is, the page takes no side.

rows.label: Prince of Peace; “of the increase of His government and peace”
rows.note: The verses speak of “a child born”; readers take them of Hezekiah, of the Messiah, or of Jesus, and the page does not choose.

rows.label: Peace upon Israel; for Jerusalem and the city
rows.note: Gal 6:16 reads “Peace and mercy to all who walk by this rule, even to the Israel of God”; where readers part on who the Israel of God is, the page takes no side. Jer 29:7 is the city of the exile.
rows._why: merged from two rows: peace upon Israel and 'pray for the peace of Jerusalem'

rows.label: What peace stands beside: righteousness, justice, truth, love, joy, the law, life and blessing
rows.note: Companions in the same verse, not claims about how they relate. Gal 5:22 is the fruit of the Spirit. Eph 2:15, which speaks of the law abolished, stands in the Christ row with its own note.
rows._why: merged from six rows (righteousness and justice; truth, loving devotion and love; joy; the law; life and blessing; the fruit of the Spirit), each verse one that row had found. Zech 8:16 stays out: the Hebrew is 'judgments of peace' and the Berean prints 'sound judgments', so the verse does not show peace beside justice or truth (it is in 'Peace in other uses'). Also left out, as before, where the Berean renders the companion word otherwise: 2 Kgs 20:19 and Isa 39:8 ('security' for 'truth'), Jer 14:13 ('lasting'), Gen 37:4 (Jacob's love, not a companion of peace)

rows.label: Peace and faith, believing

not_verses.1Tim.1.2: 'the faith' names whose child Timothy is, not what peace stands beside
not_verses.Titus.1.4: 'our common faith' names whose child Titus is, not what peace stands beside

rows.note: Where the text names faith beside peace the verse is listed as written; where traditions part on what faith does, the page takes no side.

rows.label: Seek it, pursue it, live in it: the way of peace, among the brothers, those who do good, being made holy
rows._why: merged from five rows: seek and pursue (rule: object_of רָדַף, בָּקַשׁ, דָּרַשׁ, διώκω, ζητέω), the upright and those who do good (by hand), the way and path of peace (rule), among the brothers, in the churches (rule on ἐκκλησία, ἀλλήλων, ἀδελφός; Rev 6:4 'slay one another' was taken out) and peace with being made holy (rule: ἁγιασμός, ἁγιάζω)

rows.label: Peace in other uses
rows.note: Verses the rows above do not take, among them those where the Berean’s word for the Hebrew שָׁלוֹם is not ‘peace’ (‘in triumph’, ‘wholly’, ‘a sound answer’, ‘sound judgments’) or where the Berean prints no word for it at all.

rows.label: Live at peace with one another, with everyone; “making peace through the blood of His cross”
rows.note: Live at peace is εἰρηνεύω; “making peace” in Col 1:20 is εἰρηνοποιέω. Col 1:20: where readers part on what reconciliation with God is and how it is made, the page takes no side.
rows._why: εἰρηνεύω and εἰρηνοποιέω; the Hebrew verb שָׁלַם is in the noun rows (the builder files it there)

rows.label: Peacemakers (εἰρηνοποιός); peace-loving; the peaceful fruit of discipline (εἰρηνικός)
rows.note: Two different words: εἰρηνοποιός, “peacemakers” (Matt 5:9), and εἰρηνικός, which the Berean prints “peace-loving” (Jas 3:17) and “peace” (Heb 12:11, the fruit of discipline).
rows._why: εἰρηνοποιός (Matt 5:9, which the builder files as an adjective) and εἰρηνικός (Heb 12:11, Jas 3:17)
